paraphrase: Samādhi-pāda (the chapter on samādhi), 1.1–1.51. The chapter opens by announcing the teaching of yoga (1.1) and defining it as the stilling (nirodha) of the mind's activities (vṛtti) (1.2), with the seer then abiding in its own form (1.3–1.4). It sets out the five activities, afflicted or unafflicted (1.5–1.11), and the means of stilling them, practice (abhyāsa) and dispassion (vairāgya), lower and higher (1.12–1.16). It then defines the two samādhis, with full awareness (saṃprajñāta) and beyond it (asaṃprajñāta) (1.17–1.18), gives the birth-based and means-based forms and the five means (1.19–1.22), and teaches devotion to Īśvara, his definition, and the praṇava (1.23–1.29). Next come the nine obstacles (antarāya) and their five companions (1.30–1.31), the single-principle practice against them (1.32), the four attitudes (1.33) and further supports for steadiness (1.34–1.39), followed by coalescence (samāpatti), its four kinds and the samādhi with seed (1.40–1.46), the truth-bearing insight (1.47–1.49), and the seedless samādhi in which even the impression of insight is stilled (1.50–1.51). Its purpose, as the chapter presents it, is to teach yoga to the mind that is already concentrated (samāhita-citta), as Vyāsa says at the start of the second chapter.

paraphrase: Sādhana-pāda (the chapter on the means), 2.1–2.55. The chapter turns to the practitioner whose mind is not yet concentrated (vyutthita-citta), teaching kriyā-yoga (austerity, self-study, devotion to Īśvara) (2.1–2.2). It then names the five afflictions (kleśa) (2.3), their four states (dormant, attenuated, interrupted, fully active) and the field of ignorance (2.4), each affliction in turn (2.5–2.9), and how they are to be abandoned (2.10–2.11). It gives the karma-store rooted in the afflictions, its ripening in birth, life-span and experience, and the fruit of joy or anguish (2.12–2.14), teaches that all is suffering for the discerning and that future suffering is to be avoided (2.15–2.16), and sets out the seer and the seen, their conjunction, its cause in ignorance and its ending in isolation (kaivalya) (2.17–2.25). Discriminative discernment is the means and its final insight is sevenfold (2.26–2.27). paraphrase: Chapter 3 (Vibhūti-pāda, 55 sūtras; the bhāṣya's colophon names it 'vibhūti-pāda'). (1) 3.1-3.8: the last three limbs, concentration (dhāraṇā), meditation (dhyāna) and samādhi, and saṃyama as the three on one object; mastery gives the light of insight; application by stages; the three are inner relative to the earlier limbs and outer relative to the seedless samādhi. (2) 3.9-3.15: the transformations of the mind (of restraint, of samādhi, of one-pointedness) and the transformations of property, characteristic and condition in elements and senses; the property-bearer; sequence as the cause of difference of transformation. paraphrase: Thesis of the Yoga Sūtra (with Vyāsa's bhāṣya), decided by the six marks of purport. The text teaches yoga, defined as the restraint (nirodha) of the modifications of the mind (1.2), whose result is the seer's abiding in its own form (1.3); the eight limbs (2.29) and saṃyama (3.4) are its means, discriminative vision (2.26, 3.49, 4.29) its ripening, and kaivalya (2.25, 3.50, 3.55, 4.34) its end. (1) Opening and closing (upakrama-upasaṃhāra): the text opens 'now the teaching of yoga' (1.1), defines yoga and states the seer's abiding in its own form (1.2-1.3); it closes with kaivalya as the establishment in its own form of the power of consciousness (4.34), the same abiding in its own form (svarūpa-pratiṣṭhā) as 1.3 names. (2) Repetition (abhyāsa): kaivalya is stated at 2.25, 3.50, 3.55, 4.26, 4.34; the destruction of afflictions as burnt seeds at 2.10, 3.50, 4.28; discriminative vision at 2.26, 3.49, 3.55, 4.29; the distinction between seer and seen or mind and puruṣa at 2.17-2.23, 3.35, 4.18-4.24; saṃskāra and vāsanā at 1.18, 1.50, 3.9-3.10, 4.8-4.11, 4.27-4.28. (3) Novelty (apūrvatā): no verse marks anything as novel or as knowable by no other means; the only self-designation of this kind is the bhāṣya on 3.4 calling 'saṃyama' the treatise's technical term (paribhāṣā). (4) Stated result (phala): the seer's abiding in its own form (1.3), the light of knowledge up to discriminative vision from the limbs (2.28), results attached to each restraint and observance (2.35-2.45), the results of saṃyama (3.5 and 3.16-3.49), cessation of afflictions and karma and the end of the guṇas' sequence (4.30-4.32), kaivalya (4.34). (5) Praise (arthavāda): no verse is a passage of praise as such; the long list of powers (3.16-3.49) is stated as results, and the text itself places powers below kaivalya: the perceptions of 3.36 are obstacles in samādhi (3.37), kaivalya comes from dispassion even toward overlordship and omniscience (3.50), and invitations from those of high stations are to be met without attachment or pride (3.51). Whether any passage functions as praise is left to the interpretation layer (P7). (6) Reasoned demonstration (upapatti): the account of ignorance as the cause of the conjunction of seer and seen (2.15-2.25); the transformations of the mind and elements (3.9-3.15); the argument for the existence of past and future (4.12), for an object independent of any one mind (4.14-4.16), for the mind's being seen and not self-luminous (4.19-4.21), and for puruṣa from the mind's acting in combination for another (4.24).
